mainEntity.name: Do basement walls need to be framed as floating walls, or can they be attached tight to the concrete?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Floating walls are usually the safest default for Denver-area basements because the floor slab and foundation can move a little with seasonal soil changes. A floating wall lets the framing move independently so you reduce drywall cracks and stress at the base of the wall. For most projects, that matters more than building the wall tight to the concrete.

In Denver, Centennial, Greenwood Village, Foxfield, and Parker, the right approach also depends on your basement height, moisture conditions, and whether you are adding bedrooms or other finished rooms. The framing plan should account for insulation, electrical runs, and any required egress openings before the first wall goes up.

Key factors:
- Seasonal foundation movement
- Basement moisture and slab conditions
- Finished room layout and ceiling height
- Electrical, plumbing, and insulation planning

If you are unsure, have the framing layout checked before materials are cut. That is the easiest time to avoid expensive rework later.
acceptedAnswer.description: Most Denver-area basements use floating walls so the framing can move independently from the foundation. That helps prevent drywall cracks when the slab or foundation shifts seasonally. The best setup depends on moisture, height, and the finished layout.
